evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kucinski et al., 2017.

claim: Local induction of autophagy has been suggested as a mechanism for cell competition.
source: A role for innate immune pathway components has been proposed (Meyer et al., 2014), and different levels of oxidative stress response in Rp+/- cells and Rp+/+ cells (Kucinski et al., 2017) or local induction of autophagy have also been suggested (Nagata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nagata et al., 2019.

claim: Most of the p53-independent cell death that follows irradiation resembles cell competition genetically.
source: We show that, as hypothesized previously (McNamee and Brodsky, 2009), most of the p53-independent cell death that follows irradiation resembles cell competition genetically.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: It is cell competition that removes cells heterozygous for large deletions, when they include ribosomal protein genes.
source: We then use a targeted recombination method to investigate the fate of somatic cells that acquire large-scale genetic changes directly, and confirm that it is cell competition that removes cells heterozygous for large deletions, when they include ribosomal protein genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-9.

claim: When ribosomal protein genes are unaffected, or when the cell competition pathway is inactivated genetically, cells carrying large deletions remain largely un-competed, proliferate, and contribute to adult structures.
source: By contrast, when ribosomal protein genes are unaffected, or when the cell competition pathway is inactivated genetically, cells carrying large deletions remain largely un-competed, proliferate, and contribute to adult structures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-9.

claim: Cell competition is a highly significant mechanism for elimination of aneuploid somatic cells.
source: Thus, cell competition is a highly significant mechanism for elimination of aneuploid somatic cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: Irradiating third-instar larvae resulted in rapid induction of cell death in the wing imaginal disc that was largely p53-dependent.
source: Irradiating third-instar larvae resulted in rapid induction of cell death in the wing imaginal disc that was largely p53-dependent (Figure 1A,C,D,E,G,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C,D,E,G,H.

claim: The p53-dependent cell death, attributable to the DNA-damage response, was not much affected by the rpS12G97D mutation that interferes with cell competition.
source: The p53-dependent cell death, attributable to the DNA-damage response, was not much affected by the rpS12G97D mutation that interferes with cell competition (Figure 1B,F,H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,F,H.

claim: While total cell death tailed off with time, p53-independent cell death increased around 18–24 hr post-irradiation.
source: While total cell death tailed off with time, p53-independent cell death increased around 18–24 hr post-irradiation, as reported previously (Wichmann et al., 2006; McNamee and Brodsky, 2009; Figure 1I–L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I–L and citations to previous studies.

claim: 24 hr after irradiation, p53-independent cell death was reduced by 66% in the rpS12G97D p53 double mutant compared to the p53 mutant alone.
source: As expected for cell competition, 24 hr after irradiation, p53-independent cell death was reduced by 66% in the rpS12G97D p53 double mutant compared to the p53 mutant alone (Figure 1K–M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K–M.

claim: A genomic transgene encoding wild-type rpS12 restored p53-independent cell death to the rpS12G97D p53 double mutant strain.
source: To exclude the possibility that other genetic background differences were responsible, rpS12 function was restored to the rpS12G97D p53 double mutant strain using a P element transgene encoding the wild-type rpS12 gene, and this restored p53-independent cell death (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: A genomic transgene encoding the rpS12G97D cell competition-defective allele did not restore p53-independent cell death, leading to 86% less p53-independent cell death than the wild-type rpS12 transgene.
source: Notably, a genomic transgene encoding the rpS12G97D cell competition-defective allele did not, leading to 86% less p53-independent cell death than the wild-type rpS12 transgene (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: 66–86% of the p53-independent apoptosis was RpS12-dependent and might represent cell competition.
source: Thus, 66–86% of the p53-independent apoptosis was RpS12-dependent and might represent cell competition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Twenty-four hr after irradiation, p53 mutant wing discs exhibit cells expressing nuclear Xrp1 in a pattern similar to that of dying cells.
source: Twenty-four hr after irradiation, p53 mutant wing discs exhibit cells expressing nuclear Xrp1 in a pattern similar to that of dying cells. We were unable to double-label with anti-Xrp1 and anti-active Dcp1 simultaneously because both are rabbit antisera. n: 33 (p53-); 26 (rpS12G97D p53-).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Fewer Xrp1-expressing cells were seen in rpS12G97D p53- double mutant wing discs.
source: Fewer Xrp1-expressing cells were seen in rpS12G97D p53- double mutant wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1O.

claim: Most (58%) of the p53-independent Xrp1 expression 24 hr post-irradiation was RpS12-dependent.
source: Most (58%) of the p53-independent Xrp1 expression 24 hr post-irradiation was RpS12-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1P.

claim: Irradiated adult flies show short, thin scutellar bristles like those typical of Rp+/- mutant flies.
source: Irradiated adult flies with a short, thin scutellar bristle (white arrow, compare normal contralateral bristle – black arrow) like those typical of Rp+/- mutant flies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: The frequency of sporadic Rp-like bristles increases 3.33x and 4x on the thoraces of rpS12G97D and rpS12G97D p53- flies (respectively) where cell competition is inhibited.
source: The frequency of sporadic Rp-like bristles increases 3.33x and 4x on the thoraces of rpS12G97D and rpS12G97D p53- flies (respectively) where cell competition is inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1R.

claim: The preponderance of y bristles in females following irradiation suggests that induced y mutations typically affect other genes including essential genes.
source: Frequencies of y bristles found on the thoraces of ~2000 y/+; rpS12G97D female and +/Y; rpS12G97D male flies following irradiation (1000 rad) in the mid-third larval instar. The preponderance of y bristles in females suggests that induced y mutations typically affect other genes including essential genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1S.

claim: 37.5% of y bristles in females were also phenotypically Minute, consistent with loss of chromosome regions extending at least from the y locus to the RpL36 gene.
source: In females, 37.5% of y bristles were also phenotypically Minute, consistent with loss of chromosome regions extending at least from the y locus to the RpL36 gene 0.3 Mb more centromere-proximal that is the nearest Rp locus (Figure 1S).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1S.

claim: Minute-like bristles seen following irradiation most commonly reflect loss of substantial chromosome segments including Rp genes.
source: Although this study was small scale, these findings support the conclusion from DNA repair mutant studies that Minute-like bristles seen following irradiation most commonly reflect loss of substantial chromosome segments including Rp genes, (Baker et al., 1978).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and citation to Baker et al., 1978.

claim: Many Minute-like bristles removed by cell competition genes following irradiation could represent segmentally aneuploid cells.
source: Accordingly, many Minute-like bristles removed by cell competition genes following irradiation could represent such segmentally aneuploid cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Cell competition removes ~3/4 of the cells with genetic changes that encompass dose-sensitive Rp loci that arise after irradiation.
source: Taken together, these bristle results are also consistent with the notion that cell competition removes ~3/4 of the cells with genetic changes that encompass dose-sensitive Rp loci that arise after irradiation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1R.

claim: FLP recombination between pairs of FRT elements linked in cis excises intervening sequences to make defined deletions with a single FRT remaining at the recombination site.
source: FLP recombination between pairs of FRT elements linked in cis excises intervening sequences to make defined deletions with a single FRT remaining at the recombination site (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the FLP-FRT system, illustrated in Figure 2A,B.

claim: FLP-mediated excision from paired FRT strains in the FRT w+ … w+ FRT configuration removes both the associated w+ genes, so that affected cells can be identified in the adult eye by loss of pigmentation.
source: Insertion elements of the Exelixis collection exist in several configurations, and FLP-mediated excision from paired FRT strains in the FRT w+ … w+ FRT configuration removes both the associated w+ genes, so that affected cells can be identified in the adult eye by loss of pigmentation (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, illustrated in Figure 2A,B.

claim: 17 segmentally aneuploid genotypes were cell-viable, and able to grow and differentiate in the Drosophila eye.
source: Overall, these results showed that 17 segmentally aneuploid genotypes were cell-viable, and able to grow and differentiate in the Drosophila eye, although a minority might have an effect on growth in this tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A minority of segmentally aneuploid genotypes might have an effect on growth in the eye tissue.
source: Overall, these results showed that 17 segmentally aneuploid genotypes were cell-viable, and able to grow and differentiate in the Drosophila eye, although a minority might have an effect on growth in this tissue.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Recombination in the 17 strains each deleted 1.4 Mb – 8.5 Mb of autosomal DNA, representing 1–6% of the sequenced genome each.
source: Recombination in these 17 strains each deleted 1.4 Mb – 8.5 Mb of autosomal DNA, representing 1–6% of the sequenced genome each (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3A.

claim: Together these deletions encompass 25.3 Mb of DNA, corresponding to 21.1% of the Drosophila euchromatin and 17.7% of the sequenced genome.
source: Together these deletions encompass 25.3 Mb of DNA, corresponding to 21.1% of the Drosophila euchromatin and 17.7% of the sequenced genome.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the experimental data.

claim: 11 of the 17 genotypes deleted one or more Rp loci.
source: 11 of these 17 genotypes deleted one or more Rp loci (RpS11, RpS13, RpS16, RpS20, RpS24, RpS30, RpL14, RpL18, RpL28 or RpL36A), whereas six affected no Rp gene (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3A.

claim: Six of the 17 genotypes affected no Rp gene.
source: 11 of these 17 genotypes deleted one or more Rp loci (RpS11, RpS13, RpS16, RpS20, RpS24, RpS30, RpL14, RpL18, RpL28 or RpL36A), whereas six affected no Rp gene (Supplementary file 1, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3A.

claim: Segmental aneuploidy prevented cells contributing clones to the adult eye whenever Rp gene dose was reduced.
source: As expected, segmental aneuploidy prevented cells contributing clones to the adult eye whenever Rp gene dose was reduced (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and summarized in Figure 11A.

claim: Cell competition appears to be the primary mechanism limiting the contribution of segmental aneuploidies in the tested size ranges to adult tissues.
source: More significantly, cell competition appears to be the primary mechanism limiting the contribution of segmental aneuploidies in the tested size ranges to adult tissues, because segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when they did not affect Rp loci, when diploidy for Rp loci was restored with a transgene, or when the cell competition pathway that depends on RpS12 and Xrp1 function was mutated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figures 2-9.

claim: Segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when they did not affect Rp loci.
source: More significantly, cell competition appears to be the primary mechanism limiting the contribution of segmental aneuploidies in the tested size ranges to adult tissues, because segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when they did not affect Rp loci, when diploidy for Rp loci was restored with a transgene, or when the cell competition pathway that depends on RpS12 and Xrp1 function was mutated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: Segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when diploidy for Rp loci was restored with a transgene.
source: More significantly, cell competition appears to be the primary mechanism limiting the contribution of segmental aneuploidies in the tested size ranges to adult tissues, because segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when they did not affect Rp loci, when diploidy for Rp loci was restored with a transgene, or when the cell competition pathway that depends on RpS12 and Xrp1 function was mutated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when the cell competition pathway that depends on RpS12 and Xrp1 function was mutated.
source: More significantly, cell competition appears to be the primary mechanism limiting the contribution of segmental aneuploidies in the tested size ranges to adult tissues, because segmental aneuploid cells easily survived and contributed large fractions of the adult tissue when they did not affect Rp loci, when diploidy for Rp loci was restored with a transgene, or when the cell competition pathway that depends on RpS12 and Xrp1 function was mutated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5-9.

claim: The segmentally-aneuploid genotypes examined were able to form entire heads of aneuploid cells when eyFlp was used to drive recombination in all the cells.
source: The segmental-aneuploid genotypes examined here were able to form entire heads of aneuploid cells when eyFlp was used to drive recombination in all the cells (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The removal of sporadic aneuploid cells depended on competition with diploid cells.
source: The removal of sporadic aneuploid cells therefore depended on competition with diploid cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data comparing eyFlp and hsFlp results.

claim: Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+ and Df(3L)65A5-65A9/+ genotypes were viable in all tissues when competing wild type cells were not present.
source: In fact in the cases of Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+, heterozygous for the RpS16 and RpS24 genes, and Df(3L)65A5-65A9/+, heterozygous for the RpL28 gene, we bred flies that received heat-shock recombination, and recovered non-mosaic, entirely segmentally aneuploid flies in the next generation, derived from FLP-FRT recombination in the germlines of the parents. Thus, these segmentally aneuploid genotypes, which rarely survived in sporadic clones, were viable in all tissues when competing wild type cells were not present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from breeding experiments.

claim: The most effective suppression of Rp+/- segmental aneuploid clones was generally seen when the whole animal was heterozygous for a point mutation in RpS3.
source: The most effective suppression of Rp+/- segmental aneuploid clones was generally seen when the whole animal was heterozygous for a point mutation in RpS3 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The feature of euploid cells that enables them to eliminate aneuploid cells is their Rp+/+ genotype.
source: This is further, compelling evidence that cell competition due to reduced Rp gene dose is the main mechanism eliminating segmentally aneuploid because it shows that the feature of euploid cells that enables them to eliminate aneuploid cells is their Rp+/+ genotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Segmental aneuploidy leaving Rp loci unaffected was compatible with clonal growth and differentiation for four of the five genomic regions tested.
source: In contrast to these results, segmental aneuploidy leaving Rp loci unaffected was compatible with clonal growth and differentiation for four of the five genomic regions tested (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: eIF2γ is the locus responsible for loss of Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ clones and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ clones.
source: In the exception, we identified eIF2γ as the locus responsible for loss Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ clones and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ clones (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: No point mutant alleles of the eIF2γ gene are known.
source: No point mutant alleles of the eIF2γ gene are known and the locus is believed to be haplo-lethal to Drosophila (Marygold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Marygold et al., 2007.

claim: The eIF2γ locus is believed to be haplo-lethal to Drosophila.
source: No point mutant alleles of the eIF2γ gene are known and the locus is believed to be haplo-lethal to Drosophila (Marygold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Marygold et al., 2007.

claim: It is cell competition that eliminates eIF2γ+/- aneuploid cells from the eye.
source: It is cell competition that eliminates eIF2γ+/- aneuploid cells from the eye, however, since they could form apparently normal adult heads when no diploid competitor cells were present (Figure 2P–R).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2P–R.

claim: Clones of the eIF2γ+/- genotypes Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ were restored by both the Xrp1 mutant and by the RpS3+/- mutant background.
source: Moreover, clones of the eIF2γ+/- genotypes Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ were restored by both the Xrp1 mutant and by the RpS3+/- mutant background, as expected for cell competition (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Out of 63 other translation factor genes examined in a systematic study of whole body, non-mosaic phenotypes, eIF2α and eIF2γ were the only haploinsufficient loci found.
source: Out of 63 other translation factor genes examined in a systematic study of whole body, non-mosaic phenotypes, eIF2α and eIF2γ were the only haploinsufficient loci found (Marygold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marygold et al., 2007.

claim: The eIF2α gene is the only other locus known where point mutants lead to the developmental delay and thin bristle phenotype that is otherwise typical of heterozygous Rp mutants.
source: Notably, the eIF2α gene is the only other locus known where point mutants lead to the developmental delay and thin bristle phenotype that is otherwise typical of heterozygous Rp mutants (Marygold et al., 2007), suggesting a functional relationship between Rp mutants and the eIF2 complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marygold et al., 2007.

claim: There is a functional relationship between Rp mutants and the eIF2 complex.
source: Notably, the eIF2α gene is the only other locus known where point mutants lead to the developmental delay and thin bristle phenotype that is otherwise typical of heterozygous Rp mutants (Marygold et al., 2007), suggesting a functional relationship between Rp mutants and the eIF2 complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypic similarity.

claim: eIF2α is regulated by Xrp1 and contributes directly to the cell competition mechanism.
source: Independent studies in our laboratory already indicate that eIF2α is regulated by Xrp1 and contributes directly to the cell competition mechanism (Kiparaki, Khan, Cheun and Baker, in preparation).
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data from the authors' laboratory.

claim: Cells with whole chromosome aneuploidies experience a stress associated with mismatched dose of many proteins.
source: Previous studies suggested that cells with whole chromosome aneuploidies experience a stress associated with mismatched dose of many proteins (Torres et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2018; Terhorst et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Torres et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2018; Terhorst et al., 2020.

claim: The effect of stress from mismatched protein doses must be small compared to cell competition in the segmental aneuploid cells studied.
source: We cannot measure how such stresses reduced clonal growth of segmental aneuploid cells in our experiments, but the effect must be small compared to cell competition, since without cell competition, segmental aneuploid cells easily contributed half or more of the eye, whereas cell competition drastically reduces this contribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: It is plausible that additional stresses increase with more extensive loss of genetic material.
source: It is plausible, however, that additional stresses increase with more extensive loss of genetic material, eg clones heterozygous for a 6.3 Mb deletion removing the RpL14, RpL18, and RpL28 loci were recovered less well than smaller deletions (Figure 6), as if larger monosomies experience other stresses in addition to cell competition.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Extra copies of at least two Rp genes (RpS12 and RpL36) do not trigger cell removal.
source: Since extra copies of at least two Rp genes (RpS12 and RpL36) do not trigger cell removal (Kale et al., 2018), other mechanisms would also be required to eliminate cells with triploidies, or act in tissues that lack cell competition (Ripoll, 1980).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kale et al., 2018.

claim: Other mechanisms would be required to eliminate cells with triploidies, or act in tissues that lack cell competition.
source: Since extra copies of at least two Rp genes (RpS12 and RpL36) do not trigger cell removal (Kale et al., 2018), other mechanisms would also be required to eliminate cells with triploidies, or act in tissues that lack cell competition (Ripoll, 1980).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: Preventing apoptosis of Drosophila cells that have chromosome instability leads to invasive tumor growth that can be propagated after transplantation.
source: Finally, preventing apoptosis of Drosophila cells that have chromosome instability leads to invasive tumor growth that can be propagated after transplantation (Dekanty et al., 2012; Benhra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dekanty et al., 2012 and Benhra et al., 2018.

claim: Blocking cell death of segmentally aneuploid cells did not lead to invasive growth.
source: We did not observe invasive growth after blocking cell death of segmentally aneuploid cells, suggesting that chromosome instability may lead to different classes of aneuploidy, or to other additional effects.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Chromosome instability may lead to different classes of aneuploidy, or to other additional effects.
source: We did not observe invasive growth after blocking cell death of segmentally aneuploid cells, suggesting that chromosome instability may lead to different classes of aneuploidy, or to other additional effects.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental observation.

claim: The segmental aneuploidies studied were comparable in genetic content to some whole chromosome monosomies in humans.
source: If cell competition is the main mechanism eliminating cells with segmental monosomies, at least up to a certain size, how important is this? The segmental aneuploidies we studied were comparable in genetic content to some whole chromosome monosomies in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of genetic content.

claim: Cells heterozygous for Df(2R)56F16-58E2 were hemizygous for a 2.2 Mb region including 1.5% of the genome, encoding 333 protein coding genes and 55 non-coding RNAs.
source: For example, cells heterozygous for Df(2R)56F16-58E2 were hemizygous for a 2.2 Mb region including 1.5% of the genome, about as large a region as can be expected to lack any Rp gene, encoding 333 protein coding genes and 55 non-coding RNAs.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic content of the deletion.

claim: Human chromosome 21 contains 1.5% of the genome that lacks any Rp gene, encoding 234 protein coding genes and 404 non-coding RNAs.
source: Human chromosome 21, which also contains 1.5% of the genome that lacks any Rp gene, encodes 234 protein coding genes and 404 non-coding RNAs (Uechi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Uechi et al., 2001.

claim: Df(2R)56F16-58E2 is comparable in genetic terms to loss of a small human chromosome.
source: Thus, Df(2R)56F16-58E2 is comparable in genetic terms to loss of a small human chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of genetic content.

claim: Some of the segmental aneuploidies studied in Drosophila were several-fold larger than Df(2R)56F16-58E2.
source: Some of the segmental aneuploidies we studied in Drosophila were several-fold larger than Df(2R)56F16-58E2 (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3A), Thus, our studies may best model aneuploidies affecting one or a few human chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3A.

claim: The studies may best model aneuploidies affecting one or a few human chromosomes.
source: Some of the segmental aneuploidies we studied in Drosophila were several-fold larger than Df(2R)56F16-58E2 (Supplementary file 1; Figure 3A), Thus, our studies may best model aneuploidies affecting one or a few human chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of genetic content.

claim: ~80% of the Drosophila genome is carried on two autosomes.
source: Because ~80% of the Drosophila genome is carried on two autosomes, whole-chromosome aneuploidies in Drosophila, by contrast, better mimic complex karyotypes seen in tumors or in cells with chromosome instability, which affect many chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila genome.

claim: Whole-chromosome aneuploidies in Drosophila better mimic complex karyotypes seen in tumors or in cells with chromosome instability.
source: Because ~80% of the Drosophila genome is carried on two autosomes, whole-chromosome aneuploidies in Drosophila, by contrast, better mimic complex karyotypes seen in tumors or in cells with chromosome instability, which affect many chromosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic organization.

claim: If more than half the p53-independent cell death following irradiation resembles cell competition, this suggests cell competition could be significant for removing many, although not all, the damaged cells that arise.
source: Ionizing radiation generates many kinds of chromosome aberration, so if more than half the p53-independent cell death following irradiation resembles cell competition (Figure 1), this suggests cell competition could be significant for removing many, although not all, the damaged cells that arise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The 80 Rp gene loci are distributed seemingly randomly around the 24 pairs of human chromosomes.
source: Could cell competition be important in humans? As in Drosophila, the 80 Rp gene loci are distributed seemingly randomly around the 24 pairs of human chromosomes (Uechi et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Uechi et al., 2001.

claim: At least 21 human Rp genes have been found to be haploinsufficient and are responsible for the dominant syndrome Diamond Blackfan Anemia (DBA).
source: At least 21 human Rp genes have so far been found to be haploinsufficient and are responsible for the dominant syndrome Diamond Blackfan Anemia (DBA)(Ulirsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ulirsch et al., 2018.

claim: Rp genes could be sensors for aneuploidy in humans.
source: Thus Rp genes could be sensors for aneuploidy in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the distribution of Rp genes.

claim: The retention of aneuploid cells in Drosophila that inherit an Rp mutation from the germline resembles the situation in human DBA patients.
source: The retention of aneuploid cells in Drosophila that inherit an Rp mutation from the germline (Figure 9) resembles the situation in human DBA patients, the majority of whom are constitutively heterozygous for a Rp gene mutation or deletion (Ulirsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 9 and citation to Ulirsch et al., 2018.

claim: The majority of DBA patients are constitutively heterozygous for a Rp gene mutation or deletion.
source: The retention of aneuploid cells in Drosophila that inherit an Rp mutation from the germline (Figure 9) resembles the situation in human DBA patients, the majority of whom are constitutively heterozygous for a Rp gene mutation or deletion (Ulirsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ulirsch et al., 2018.

claim: DBA patients experience 4.8x higher lifetime incidence of multiple cancers, not limited to the hematopoietic system.
source: DBA patients experience 4.8x higher lifetime incidence of multiple cancers, not limited to the hematopoietic system (Vlachos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vlachos et al., 2018.

claim: DBA patients might experience a diminished capacity to recognize and eliminate aneuploid cells, because their euploid cells are not Rp+/+.
source: To these we can now add the possibility that DBA patients experience a diminished capacity to recognize and eliminate aneuploid cells, because their euploid cells are not Rp+/+(Figure 11B).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: If DBA patients have diminished capacity to eliminate aneuploid cells, cell competition might remove as many as 80% of pre-neoplastic cells from normal individuals due to their aneuploidy.
source: The nearly fivefold increase in tumor incidence suggests that if this was correct, cell competition might remove as many as 80% of pre-neoplastic cells from normal individuals due to their aneuploidy, This seems comparable to our findings that cell competition removes 58–86% of the cells with radiation-damaged genomes in Drosophila(Figure 1M,P,R).
evidence: This is a speculative calculation based on the tumor incidence in DBA patients and the experimental data.

claim: Cell competition removes 58–86% of the cells with radiation-damaged genomes in Drosophila.
source: The nearly fivefold increase in tumor incidence suggests that if this was correct, cell competition might remove as many as 80% of pre-neoplastic cells from normal individuals due to their aneuploidy, This seems comparable to our findings that cell competition removes 58–86% of the cells with radiation-damaged genomes in Drosophila(Figure 1M,P,R).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M,P,R.

claim: A 5.6 kb genomic DNA transgene encompassing the RpL28 locus completely rescued the survival of cell clones heterozygous for Df(3L)63A3-65A9.
source: To test this in a specific case, 5.6 kb of genomic DNA encompassing the RpL28 locus was introduced onto the second chromosome using PhiC31-mediated transgenesis. This transgene proved completely sufficient to rescue the survival of cell clones heterozygous for Df(3L)63A3-65A9, a deletion of 3.2 Mb including the RpL28 locus (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: Clones of Df(3L)63A3-65A9 heterozygous cells barely survived alone, with a median contribution of 2% to the eyes of males and 0% to females.
source: Clones of Df(3L)63A3-65A9 heterozygous cells barely survived alone, with a median contribution of 2% to the eyes of males and 0% to females (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In the presence of the RpL28+ transgene, Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ clones survived in 49 out of 50 eyes, with median contributions of 37% of the eye in males and 53% in females.
source: In the presence of the RpL28+ transgene, however, Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ clones survived in 49 out of 50 eyes, with median contributions of 37% of the eye in males and 53% in females, not statistically different from clones heterozygous for Df(3L)63C1-65A9, an overlapping deletion of 3.0 Mb excluding the RpL28 locus (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: RpL28 gene dose alone determined whether a segmentally aneuploid genotype affecting hundreds of genes would be eliminated in competition with diploid cells.
source: Thus in this case, RpL28 gene dose alone determined whether a segmentally aneuploid genotype affecting hundreds of genes would be eliminated in competition with diploid cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: An 11.5 kb genomic transgene including the eIF2γ locus completely rescued the growth and differentiation of Df87B8-89B16/+ and Df87B8-89E5/+ cells to the levels typical for aneuploidies not affecting Rp genes.
source: Since independent studies in our laboratory already identified a role for the eIF2α protein in cell competition (Kiparaki, Khan, Chuen and Baker, in preparation), we tested the possible role of eIF2γ by restoring eIF2γ diploidy to Df87B8-89B16/+ or Df87B8-89E5/+ cells using a 11.5 kb genomic transgene including the eIF2γ locus (Tschiersch et al., 1994). This completely rescued the growth and differentiation of these cells to the levels typical for aneuploidies not affecting Rp genes (Figure 4D–G,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D–G,I.

claim: The locus encoding the translation factor eIF2γ behaved similarly to an Rp gene in triggering competitive elimination of heterozygous cells.
source: Thus, the locus encoding the translation factor eIF2γ behaved similarly to an Rp gene in triggering competitive elimination of heterozygous cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The normal diploid complement of Rp loci is important for sporadic segmentally aneuploid cells to evade cell competition.
source: If these studies, which tested a significant fraction of the Drosophila genome, are representative, they indicate that the normal diploid complement of Rp loci is important for sporadic segmentally aneuploid cells to evade cell competition, and that few other genes are comparably important.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: Few genes other than Rp genes are comparably important for sporadic segmentally aneuploid cells to evade cell competition.
source: If these studies, which tested a significant fraction of the Drosophila genome, are representative, they indicate that the normal diploid complement of Rp loci is important for sporadic segmentally aneuploid cells to evade cell competition, and that few other genes are comparably important.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: Elimination of Rp+/- point-mutant cells by competition depends on apoptosis.
source: If the segmentally aneuploid cells were competed by virtue of their Rp+/- genotypes, the genetic pathways should be similar. Elimination of Rp+/- point-mutant cells by competition depends on apoptosis and is suppressed by a genetic deletion, Df(3L)H99, that removes three pro-apoptotic genes reaper (rpr), grim, and head-involution defective (hid)(Moreno et al., 2002; Kale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moreno et al., 2002 and Kale et al., 2015.

claim: Elimination of Rp+/- point-mutant cells by competition is suppressed by Df(3L)H99, which removes three pro-apoptotic genes reaper (rpr), grim, and head-involution defective (hid).
source: If the segmentally aneuploid cells were competed by virtue of their Rp+/- genotypes, the genetic pathways should be similar. Elimination of Rp+/- point-mutant cells by competition depends on apoptosis and is suppressed by a genetic deletion, Df(3L)H99, that removes three pro-apoptotic genes reaper (rpr), grim, and head-involution defective (hid)(Moreno et al., 2002; Kale et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moreno et al., 2002 and Kale et al., 2015.

claim: The pro-apoptotic genes rpr, grim, and hid are required for the p53-independent cell death that follows irradiation.
source: These genes are also required for the p53-independent cell death that follows irradiation, much of which resembles cell competition (Figure 1; McNamee and Brodsky, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citation to McNamee and Brodsky, 2009.

claim: Recovery of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ cell clones was enhanced by genetic suppression of apoptosis in the Df(3L)H99/+ background.
source: Using the Df(3L)63A3-65A9, where clone loss was demonstrably due to heterozygosity for the RpL28 gene (Figure 4H), we found that recovery of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ cell clones was enhanced by genetic suppression of apoptosis in the Df(3L)H99/+ background that experiences loss of heterozygosity for rpr, grim, and hid (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: A similar rescue was obtained with the Df(3L)63C1-65F5, which deletes the RpL18 locus.
source: A similar rescue was obtained with the Df(3L)63C1-65F5, which deletes the RpL18 locus (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: The recoveries of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/Df(3L)H99 clones and Df(3L)63C1-65F5/Df(3L)H99 clones approached that of the overlapping genotype Df(3L)63C1-65A5/Df(3L)H99, in which no Rp genes were affected.
source: The recoveries of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/Df(3L)H99 clones and Df(3L)63C1-65F5/Df(3L)H99 clones approached that of the overlapping genotype Df(3L)63C1-65A5/Df(3L)H99, in which no Rp genes were affected (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,D.

claim: Pro-apoptotic genes contribute significantly to eliminating segmentally aneuploid cells.
source: In any case, it is clear from our results that pro-apoptotic genes contribute significantly to eliminating segmentally aneuploid cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Heterozygosity for an Xrp1 mutation greatly restored contribution of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ clones (RpL28+/-) to the eye.
source: Beginning with the Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ genotype where clone loss was demonstrably due to heterozygosity for the RpL28 gene (Figure 4H), we found that heterozygosity for an Xrp1 mutation greatly restored contribution of Df(3L)63A3-65A9/+ clones (RpL28+/-) to the eye (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Similar results were seen for the Df(3L)63C1-65F5/+ genotype that is heterozygous for RpL18.
source: Similar results were seen for the Df(3L)63C1-65F5/+ genotype that is heterozygous for RpL18, but Xrp1 heterozgosity did not affect recovery of clones of the overlapping Df(3L)63C1-65A9/+ that is Rp+/+ (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Xrp1 heterozygosity did not affect recovery of clones of the overlapping Df(3L)63C1-65A9/+ that is Rp+/+.
source: Similar results were seen for the Df(3L)63C1-65F5/+ genotype that is heterozygous for RpL18, but Xrp1 heterozgosity did not affect recovery of clones of the overlapping Df(3L)63C1-65A9/+ that is Rp+/+ (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: The Xrp1 mutation improved the survival of larger segmental-aneuploidies where combinations of the RpL18, RpL28, and RpL14 genes were affected.
source: The Xrp1 mutation even improved the survival of larger segmental-aneuploidies where combinations of the RpL18, RpL28, and RpL14 genes were affected (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: rpS12G97D homozygosity led to significant recovery of Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+ clones that were heterozygous for RpS16 and RpS24.
source: As expected, rpS12G97D homozygosity also led to significant recovery of Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+ clones that were heterozygous for RpS16 and RpS24, although to a quantitatively lesser degree than Xrp1 (Figure 7C,D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The contribution of Df(2R)56F16-58E2/+ cells, where no Rp gene is affected, was unaltered by the rpS12G97D mutation.
source: The contribution of Df(2R)56F16-58E2/+ cells, where no Rp gene is affected, was unaltered by the rpS12G97D mutation (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Xrp1 mutations had a minor but statistically significant effect on clones of Df(2R)48B2-50C1/+ cells, heterozygous for RpS11.
source: Xrp1 mutations had a minor but statistically significant effect on clones of Df(2R)48B2-50C1/+ cells, heterozygous for RpS11 (Figure 8A,D), a genotype that also had an autonomous effect on eye growth (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,D.

claim: Xrp1 mutations enhanced the contributions of Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ cells that were heterozygous for the eIF2γ gene.
source: Xrp1 mutations enhanced the contributions of Df(3R)87B8-89B16/+ and Df(3R)87B8-89E5/+ cells that were heterozygous for the eIF2γ gene (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B–D.

claim: Crossing to Xrp1 only slightly improved survival of Df(3R)87B8-93A2/+ clones that were heterozygous for the eIF2γ, RpS20 and RpS30 genes.
source: Crossing to Xrp1 only slightly improved survival of Df(3R)87B8-93A2/+ clones that were heterozygous for the eIF2γ, RpS20 and RpS30 genes, and did little to enhance recovery of Df(3R)89B13-93A2/+ genotypes that were heterozygous for RpS20 and RpS30 alone.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B–D.

claim: Df(3R)87B8-93A2/+ and Df(3R)89B13-93A2/+ deficiencies delete the Xrp1 locus itself.
source: As these deficiencies already delete the Xrp1 locus itself (within 91D3-5 region), introducing an Xrp1 mutation in trans leads to Xrp1-/- genotypes (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is a description of the genotypes.

claim: Heterozygous mutation of Xrp1 is sufficient to suppress competition of Rp+/- point mutant cells.
source: Heterozygous mutation of Xrp1 is already sufficient to suppress competition of Rp+/- point mutant cells (Lee et al., 2018), probably explaining why Xrp1 homozygosity had little further effect.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: Cells heterozygous at two Rp loci do not suffer more severe competition than cells heterozygous for only one Rp mutation.
source: It is known from previous work that cells heterozygous at two Rp loci do not suffer more severe competition than cells heterozygous for only one Rp mutation, and therefore that cells heterozygous for two Rp loci generally cannot be eliminated by cells heterozygous at only one Rp locus (Simpson and Morata, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simpson and Morata, 1981.

claim: Cells heterozygous for two Rp loci generally cannot be eliminated by cells heterozygous at only one Rp locus.
source: It is known from previous work that cells heterozygous at two Rp loci do not suffer more severe competition than cells heterozygous for only one Rp mutation, and therefore that cells heterozygous for two Rp loci generally cannot be eliminated by cells heterozygous at only one Rp locus (Simpson and Morata, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simpson and Morata, 1981.

claim: Clones of segmental aneuploid cells affecting various Rp genes were all recovered significantly better in an RpS3 point mutant background.
source: Accordingly, clones of segmental aneuploid cells affecting the RpS11, RpS13, RpS16, RpS20, RpS24, RpS30, RpL14, RpL18, RpL28, or RpL36A genes were all recovered significantly better in an RpS3 point mutant background, ie RpS3+/- Df(Rp)/+ clones were not eliminated from RpS3+/- tissues (Figure 9A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A,B,D.

claim: Segmental aneuploid clones heterozygous for eIF2γ were recovered significantly better in an RpS3 point mutant background.
source: This applied to segmental aneuploid clones heterozygous for eIF2γ as well (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: The RpS3 point mutant background usually had no effect on the survival of clones of genotypes that did not delete other Rp loci.
source: On the other hand, the RpS3 point mutant background usually had no effect on the survival of clones of genotypes that did not delete other Rp loci (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Df(2L)26A1-28C3/+ cells were recovered significantly better in the RpS3+/- background.
source: One exception was Df(2L)26A1-28C3/+, for which the RpS3+/- background generated significantly larger clones (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: Df(2L)26A1-28C3/+ might be subject to a mild cell competition that can be rescued in the RpS3+/- background.
source: Although this could also have reflected a lower rate of FLP-recombination between the 26A1 and 28C3 FRT sites, in the RpS3+/- background the recovery of Df2(2L)6A1-28C3/+ clones was similar to that of Df(2R)48F6-50C1/+, Df(2R)56F16-58E2/+ or Df(3L)63C1-65A9/+, suggesting instead that Df(2L)26A1-28C3/+ might be subject to a mild cell competition that can be rescued in the RpS3+/- background (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Suppressing apoptosis was least effective at expanding the contribution of aneuploid cells in the rescued eyes.
source: Although suppression of apoptosis, mutation of cell competition genes, or a germline-inherited RpS3 background all restored the growth and survival of cells hemizygous for Rp loci, they may not have done so equally. Suppressing apoptosis was least effective at expanding the contribution of aneuploid cells in the rescued eyes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Xrp1, rpS12G97D, and the RpS3+/- background suppressed cell competition to similar extents.
source: Xrp1, rpS12G97D, and the RpS3+/- background suppressed cell competition to similar extents, although the general RpS3 background often had the greatest effect, comparable to those of RpL28+ and eIF2γ+ transgenes (see statistical comparisons for the 63A3-65F5 and 56F16-59B1 regions in Figures 5 and 6 legends).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical comparisons described in the figure legends.

claim: Df(3L)H99, which suppresses apoptosis with no known increase translation or cellular growth, is expected to suppress the competition of Rp+/- cells but not restore their translation.
source: Thus Df(3L)H99, which suppresses apoptosis with no known increase translation or cellular growth, is expected to suppress the competition of Rp+/- cells but not restore their translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of Df(3L)H99.

claim: Clones of Rp+/- Df(H99)/+ cells, although surviving, are not expected to grow as rapidly or contribute as much to the eye as clones of Rp+/+ cells.
source: As a consequence, clones of Rp+/- Df(H99)/+ cells, although surviving, are not expected to grow as rapidly or contribute as much to the eye as clones of Rp+/+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected effects of suppressing apoptosis without restoring translation.

claim: The rpS12G97D and Xrp1 mutations restore the general translation rate of Rp+/- cells.
source: By contrast the rpS12G97D and Xrp1 mutations restore the general translation rate of Rp+/- cells, with Xrp1 mutation also restoring more normal rates of cellular and organismal growth (Lee et al., 2018; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2018 and Ji et al., 2019.

claim: Xrp1 mutation restores more normal rates of cellular and organismal growth to Rp+/- cells.
source: By contrast the rpS12G97D and Xrp1 mutations restore the general translation rate of Rp+/- cells, with Xrp1 mutation also restoring more normal rates of cellular and organismal growth (Lee et al., 2018; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2018 and Ji et al., 2019.

claim: A background mutation in RpS3 is not expected to restore translation or growth to segmentally aneuploid cells, but by equally impairing the unrecombined cells, and systemically delaying the growth and developmental rate of the organism as a whole, it equalizes the contributions of aneuploid and control genotypes.
source: A background mutation in RpS3 is not expected to restore translation or growth to segmentally aneuploid cells, but by equally impairing the unrecombined cells, and systemically delaying the growth and developmental rate of the organism as a whole, it equalizes the contributions of aneuploid and control genotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expected effects of a germline RpS3 mutation.

claim: The growth and survival of most segmentally aneuploid regions is determined by cell competition according to Rp gene copy number.
source: In summary, our results strongly support the conclusion that the growth and survival of most segmentally aneuploid regions is determined by cell competition according to Rp gene copy number, and show that the RpS12/Xrp1-dependent process that eliminates Rp+/- point mutated cells also acts on cells with large losses of genetic material that include Rp genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: The RpS12/Xrp1-dependent process that eliminates Rp+/- point mutated cells also acts on cells with large losses of genetic material that include Rp genes.
source: In summary, our results strongly support the conclusion that the growth and survival of most segmentally aneuploid regions is determined by cell competition according to Rp gene copy number, and show that the RpS12/Xrp1-dependent process that eliminates Rp+/- point mutated cells also acts on cells with large losses of genetic material that include Rp genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: Minute-like bristles were not observed on the thoraces of heat-shocked flies carrying Df(2R)56F16-58E2 heterozygous clones, which affect no Rp locus.
source: Minute-like bristles were not observed on the thoraces of heat-shocked flies carrying Df(2R)56F16-58E2 heterozygous clones, which affect no Rp locus, or on the thoraces of heat-shocked 56F16-59B1 flies lacking rpS12 or Xrp1 mutations, but they represented 0.5% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ rpS12G97D flies and 0.25% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ Xrp1m2-73/+ background (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: Minute-like bristles represented 0.5% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ rpS12G97D flies.
source: Minute-like bristles were not observed on the thoraces of heat-shocked flies carrying Df(2R)56F16-58E2 heterozygous clones, which affect no Rp locus, or on the thoraces of heat-shocked 56F16-59B1 flies lacking rpS12 or Xrp1 mutations, but they represented 0.5% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ rpS12G97D flies and 0.25% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ Xrp1m2-73/+ background (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: Minute-like bristles represented 0.25% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ Xrp1m2-73/+ background.
source: Minute-like bristles were not observed on the thoraces of heat-shocked flies carrying Df(2R)56F16-58E2 heterozygous clones, which affect no Rp locus, or on the thoraces of heat-shocked 56F16-59B1 flies lacking rpS12 or Xrp1 mutations, but they represented 0.5% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ rpS12G97D flies and 0.25% of the thoracic bristles in the 56F16-59B1/+ Xrp1m2-73/+ background (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+ cells survive to adulthood in the thorax if cell competition is suppressed.
source: These findings indicate that Df(2R)56F16-59B1/+ cells also survive to adulthood in the thorax if cell competition is suppressed, albeit at lower frequency than observed in the eye.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 10.
